name: watchman
intent: Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies.
problem: Message systems fail silently in the one way no error handler observes: nothing arrives. A producer stops emitting, a consumer stops draining, a scheduled job never fires, a credential expires, a partition goes offline - and because no failing code path is ever entered, error dashboards stay green while downstream data quietly goes stale. The recurring trigger: a flow whose absence is business-visible (a nightly feed, an order stream, a partner interface) has no owner-facing signal for 'no messages', so the gap is discovered late - by a customer or a downstream job - instead of by the team that can fix it.
context: Applies wherever messages are expected on a knowable cadence (event streams, queues, batch hand-offs, partner interfaces, device check-ins) and their absence is a business-visible failure: the flow has an owner, the expected period and grace window can be derived from a downstream deadline, and either the transport can be observed passively (queue counters, a wire tap) or the producers can emit out-of-band heartbeats. The watchman sits at message-flow or boundary scope - an in-process watcher beside the consumer, a periodic sweep over persisted last-seen state, or a rule in the monitoring stack fed by metrics - and it must itself be watched, because a silent watchman is exactly the failure it exists to catch.
benefits: Catches the silent failure modes nothing else reports: stalled consumer, dead producer, job that was never scheduled, expired credentials, full disk, paused partition - all of which emit no error at all.
Converts 'no news' into an explicit signal with a name, an owner and a deadline, so the gap is found within the grace window instead of by a customer days later.
Keeps observation out of the business flow: passive taps or out-of-band heartbeats let producers and consumers stay unaware of monitoring, and the escalation policy can change without touching them.

Makes expectations reviewable data: expected cadence, grace, severity and owner are declared per subject instead of living in operators' heads, which is also where a looming SLA breach becomes visible early.

Bounds detection time by design: the alarm arrives at last-arrival + period + grace, so the worst case is a property of the configuration rather than of luck - and it composes with automatic reactions (retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead) when wired to a corrective action.
Improves diagnosis when paired with a wire tap or message history: the silence alarm says when the flow stopped, the tap says what the last thing that flowed looked like.
tradeoffs: Expected silence is the default failure mode of the monitor itself: nights, weekends, batch windows and seasonal traffic turn a fixed threshold into a false-alarm generator, so per-subject calibration and quiet periods are ongoing maintenance rather than a one-off setup.

The signal is ambiguous by construction: absence cannot distinguish 'nothing to send' from 'producer dead', so expectations must come from business deadlines and the pattern needs domain input and an owner - infrastructure alone cannot supply either.

Liveness traffic costs messages and can pollute the flow it measures: heartbeats on the business channel inflate counts, break schema-strict consumers, can land in the dead-letter channel, and a heartbeat emitted by an unrelated part of the process proves process liveness rather than data-path liveness.

The watchman and its alert path become new single points of failure: if the monitor dies silently the system looks healthier than before it was added, so the pattern is only honest when it monitors itself (an always-firing watchdog alert or an external dead-man's switch) - which doubles the alerting plumbing.

One broker or network outage silences many subjects at once: without grouping, deduplication, suppression and severity mapping the watchman produces an alert storm exactly when operators are busiest, and the resulting fatigue is how the next real stall gets ignored.

The alarm state machine carries real complexity: debounce the first miss, repeat while silent, clear on recovery, and survive a watchman restart - omitting any of these yields a monitor that flaps, pages once and then goes deaf, or forgets that it had already alarmed.

participants.responsibility: The channel, queue, endpoint, scheduled feed or device population whose silence is meaningful; it owns the expected cadence, the severity and the owner who must be told.

The passive evidence (counter, wire tap, last-seen stamp) or the active messages (heartbeats, test messages) that prove the flow is still moving; it must observe the data path, not merely the process.
Holds the per-subject expectation and last-seen state, compares arrivals against the cadence - on a schedule or by waiting on a deadline - and decides when the silence has outlasted the grace window.
The declared per-subject period, grace window, quiet hours, severity, repeat interval and owner that turn a raw absence into a judgement; maintained and reviewed like code.

Delivers the alarm on the right channel with grouping, deduplication, suppression and an escalation ladder, and optionally triggers a corrective action; separate from detection so routing can change independently.
An always-firing watchdog alert or an external dead-man's switch that alarms when the watchman's own heartbeat stops arriving, so a silent monitor cannot masquerade as a healthy system.

use_cases: Nightly batch or ETL feed: page the integration owner when the 02:00 import has produced no messages by its deadline, instead of noticing an empty report at the morning stand-up.
Business-critical event stream (orders, payments, telemetry): alarm when the produce rate stays at zero through business hours, which separates a healthy quiet topic from a stopped producer.
External partner interface: notify when no messages have arrived from a B2B partner within the agreed window, turning a looming SLA breach into an early, actionable alert.
Long-running workflow stage: require a heartbeat from each process-manager step so a stuck instance is noticed before the surrounding batch closes or a compensation becomes necessary.
Retry or dead-letter pump: verify that the pump still drains failed messages - silence means the pump died, not that the backlog is empty.
Fleet check-ins (edge devices, agents, cron jobs on many hosts): raise a per-device or per-site alarm when scheduled check-ins stop arriving.
The alerting pipeline itself: an always-firing watchdog alert routed to an external service, so a broken alert path is discovered by its silence.

Cron and scheduled-job fleet via Healthchecks.io: each job pings a unique URL, the service holds the Period and Grace Time, flips the check Late then Down when no ping arrives by period + grace, and notifies integrations.

Dashboard alert rules in Grafana: an alert rule whose query returns no series enters the No Data state and can raise a DatasourceNoData alert - the platform form of deciding what silence means (No Data, Alerting, Normal or Keep last state).

Apache Burrow for Kafka (LinkedIn): committed offsets are evaluated per partition over a sliding window and a consumer is classified STALLED when its offset is frozen with non-zero lag, or STOPPED when no new commits arrive - consumer-silence detection without fixed lag thresholds.
avoid_when: You only need to know whether a process or host is up: a health-check endpoint, readiness/liveness probe or supervisor is the simpler, correct tool - flow liveness is a different question.
The monitoring stack already covers the gap (consumer-lag alarm, queue-depth alarm with an owner): fix and reuse that rule instead of adding a second, competing silence detector.

Failures are loud and immediate (synchronous calls that return errors): timeout, retry with backoff and circuit breaker are the direct tools, while absence monitoring adds detection latency by design.
The flow is genuinely bursty or unpredictable with no derivable cadence: start from volume/rate alerts or ask the producer to emit heartbeats; a raw 'no messages' threshold will only produce noise.
No owner would act on the alert: monitoring without an owner turns an operational gap into permanent noise - assign ownership before instrumenting.
anti_patterns: Watchman without meta-monitoring: the silence detector (or its alert path) dies and the system looks healthier than before the pattern was added.

Fixed absence threshold without per-subject expectations: 'alert if no messages for 5 minutes' on a nightly feed pages every night until the team mutes the alert - threshold theater that trains people to ignore alarms.
A liveness signal that proves the wrong thing: a keep-alive emitted by an unrelated scheduler loop keeps the process looking alive while the consumer is stuck; the signal must travel the data path.
Per-channel pager with no grouping or suppression: a broker outage fires every subject at once, the storm drowns the incident, and the next real stall is missed.
Alerting into the void: alarms posted to a chat channel with no owner, severity or escalation ladder, so the pattern's promise - someone is told - is never kept.
Heartbeats on the production channel: control traffic mixed into business messages inflates counts, breaks schema-strict consumers and can end up in the dead-letter channel.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: detection (expectation plus last-seen state), notification and reaction are separate; the watchman observes and reports and does not repair.
Fail-visible: absence of a signal must be a first-class monitored event, and the monitor's own failure must be observable - no silent monitors.
Explicitness: cadence, grace, severity and ownership are declared data reviewed with the code, not tribal knowledge.
Single responsibility and least knowledge: the watcher knows the flow's cadence, not its payload, and producers need not know the escalation policy.
Derive thresholds from business deadlines (from the SLA backwards) rather than from what is easy to measure.
best_practices: Derive the period and grace window from the downstream business deadline, keep grace above the observed p99 inter-arrival jitter, and re-review both when traffic patterns or SLAs change.
Stamp liveness on a monotonic clock (steady_clock, nanoTime, CLOCK_MONOTONIC, performance.now, Instant); wall-clock timestamps cause phantom silences and alarms that can never fire.
Debounce the first miss, repeat the alert while the silence persists and clear the state on recovery; make that state machine explicit and persist or re-seed it across watchman restarts.
Group, deduplicate and suppress by cause (broker outage, deployment window, planned maintenance) and map every subject to a severity and an owner before adding it.

Instrument passively where possible (queue counters, consumer lag, Wire Tap); when heartbeats are unavoidable, route them out of band on a Control Bus and make them prove the data path, as a Test Message does.
Monitor the monitor with an always-firing watchdog alert or an external dead-man's switch, and test the watchman with an injected clock plus a deliberately quiet canary subject.
Keep the watched set small and owned: fewer, aggregated subjects with clear escalation beat a per-channel firehose, and each subject must have someone who acts on its alarm.

Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns 2 - Heartbeat conversation pattern: a component sends periodic heartbeats and an observer detects the missing heartbeat and triggers an alert or corrective action: https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/conversation/HeartBeat.html

Prometheus Operator runbooks, Watchdog alert - an alert that is always firing so that its absence reveals a broken alerting pipeline: https://runbooks.prometheus-operator.dev/runbooks/general/watchdog/

Healthchecks.io documentation - periodic check-ins with a period and a grace time, transitioning to a Down state and notifying integrations when the signal does not arrive: https://healthchecks.io/docs/

Amazon CloudWatch, alarms - configurable treatment of missing data, which is the platform form of the absence decision: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch_Alarms.html
Prometheus, Alertmanager configuration - routing, grouping, inhibition and silencing of alerts, the escalation half of the pattern: https://prometheus.io/docs/alerting/latest/configuration/

Healthchecks.io, Configuring checks - simple and cron schedules with Period and Grace Time that move a check to Late and then Down when the ping does not arrive: https://healthchecks.io/docs/configuring_checks/

Grafana documentation, No Data and Error states - alert rule evaluation when a query returns no data points, with configurable transitions (No Data, Alerting, Normal, Keep last state): https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/alerting/fundamentals/alert-rule-evaluation/nodata-and-error-states/

Grafana documentation, Handle missing data in Grafana Alerting - No Data and Missing Series do not fire alerts unless the rule is configured to do so, and how DatasourceNoData alerts are named and routed: https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/alerting/guides/missing-data/

LinkedIn Engineering, Burrow: Kafka Consumer Monitoring Reinvented - sliding-window evaluation of committed offsets classifying Kafka consumer partitions OK, WARNING, STALLED or STOPPED without fixed lag thresholds: https://engineering.linkedin.com/apache-kafka/burrow-kafka-consumer-monitoring-reinvented

Apache Burrow wiki, Consumer Lag Evaluation Rules - the per-partition rules that mark a consumer STALLED (frozen offset with non-zero lag) or STOPPED (no new commits): https://github.com/linkedin/Burrow/wiki/Consumer-Lag-Evaluation-Rules

Abstractopedia, Heartbeat and Suspicion Detector - treating missed heartbeats as graded, revisable suspicion rather than confirmed death, and gating irreversible actions on that distinction: https://abstractopedia.org/mechanisms/heartbeat_and_suspicion_detector/
